indigenous.localTerm.BZ|Belize: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER profile records that Belize has many ethnic groups and languages but no consistent set of laws or policies addressing that diversity in the classroom, and the Education and Training Act names no category for them, mentioning language only in its clause on refusal of admission.

indigenous.standing.AG|Antigua and Barbuda: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act 2008 names language only among what schooling must promote understanding of, and PEER's linguistic and ethnic groups section is about special educational needs rather than any standing.
indigenous.standing.BB|Barbados: Not established from the sources consulted. The ministry's Reimagining Education reform paper roots schooling in Bajan values and respect for cultural heritage without giving the vernacular any standing, and PEER's language section for Barbados covers only conversational Spanish taught as a foreign language.
indigenous.standing.VC|Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER profile, drawing on the country's own Education For All 2015 National Review, records that there are no distinct ethnic minorities despite the heterogeneity of the population, and describes relative equity and equality in access to the education system rather than any language provision.

indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.AG|Antigua and Barbuda: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act 2008 carries no medium-of-instruction provision, and PEER treats a home language different from the language of teaching as a care point in assessment, not as a medium.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.BB|Barbados: Not established from the sources consulted. Neither the Reimagining Education reform paper nor the PEER profile names a language of instruction, and PEER's only language provision is a primary-school programme in conversational Spanish as a foreign language.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.CN|Hainan: Not established from the sources consulted. A 2017 Legal Daily report carried on the National People's Congress site states that Hainan's ethnic minority cities and counties have not brought Li-language teaching into primary and secondary classrooms, and records an NPC deputy asking government departments to introduce Chinese-Li bilingual teaching in Li areas. No provincial instrument making any locally spoken language a medium of instruction was located.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.CU|Cuba: Not established from the sources consulted. Article 2 of the 2019 Constitution makes Spanish the official language and names no other, carrying no medium-of-instruction provision, and PEER publishes no Inclusion chapter for Cuba at all.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.GG|Guernsey: Not established from the sources consulted. The Committee for Education, Sport & Culture's 2020 policy letter sets out what the new Guernsey Language Commission is expected to do in schools, and the school measures it lists are support and improvement of existing extracurricular teaching of Guernesiais in primary schools and encouragement of it as an enrichment activity in secondary schools. Neither the policy letter, the States debate of 21 August 2020 nor the 2022 media release describes Guernesiais being used to teach anything else.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.JO|Jordan: Not established from the sources consulted. At Jordan's 2012 CERD review the Country Rapporteur recorded that the state report carried limited information on how ethnic minorities had access to education in their own language, and no source consulted names a school where a language other than Arabic is the medium.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.JP|Japan: Not established from the sources consulted. The Ainu Policy Promotion Act and the Cabinet Secretariat's five-year review of it place Ainu language work under culture promotion rather than schooling, and the UNESCO PEER profile of Japan records that there is relatively little support for ethnic schools. No source located names any language other than Japanese as a medium of instruction.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.KR|South Korea: Not established from the sources consulted. Article 13 of the Jeju Language Preservation and Promotion Ordinance provides for school education for the language's preservation and dissemination, has the Superintendent support related activities at schools of every level, and lets the governor fund that teaching within the budget, but sets no medium of instruction; the Framework Act on the Korean Language is the instrument above it and names Korean.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.MU|Mauritius: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Mauritius places Kreol Morisien in the curriculum only as an optional language subject, and records the Ministry's view that pupils should be able to learn and be assessed in the spoken language 'rather than the medium of instruction', which implies Kreol is not itself the medium; the profile names no medium of instruction and no grade boundary. Searched: PEER Mauritius inclusion profile.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.SV|El Salvador: Not established from the sources consulted. The ministry records training 85 teachers in Nahuat to promote teaching of the language, not teaching in it, and PEER records the 2015 indigenous peoples policy proposing curricular changes to include knowledge of indigenous culture rather than any medium of instruction.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.UY|Uruguay: Not established from the sources consulted. The only source on this entry is Ley 18.437, Ley General de Educación (IMPO). No medium-of-instruction rule for the three was found in the cited source.
indigenous.mediumOfInstruction.VC|Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act 2006 carries no medium-of-instruction provision, naming language only among what schooling should promote understanding of and in the English Language pass required of teachers, and the Garifuna Heritage Foundation's 2024 programme runs teacher workshops and cultural exchanges without naming any classroom language.

indigenous.taughtAsSubject.AO|Angola: Not established from the sources consulted. Lei n.º 17/16 treats Angolan languages only as a complement and learning instrument alongside Portuguese-medium teaching (Art. 16) and names their valorisation among the aims of the adult-education subsystem (Art. 53); it creates no timetabled national-language subject in general education. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Angola carries no ethnic-and-linguistic-groups section. Searched: full text of Lei 17/16, PEER Angola inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.BA|Bosnia and Herzegovina: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key Data on Teaching Languages at School in Europe (2023 edition, policy position 2021/22) places Bosnia and Herzegovina among the countries that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities, so no regional or minority language is named as a school subject at that level. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all three state languages on the same source's Figure A1.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.BB|Barbados: Not established from the sources consulted. The Ministry of Education's own reform document Reimagining Education in Barbados sets out the current primary core curriculum as English, Mathematics, Social Studies, Science, Physical Education, Art, Music, Religious Knowledge and Health and Family Life Education, and the only language addition it proposes at pre-primary and primary level is "functional foreign languages"; no subject in the local vernacular appears. The UNESCO PEER profile for Barbados records under Language only a conversational Spanish programme in primary schools, taught as a foreign language.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.BE|Belgium — French Community (Wallonia-: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key data on teaching languages at school in Europe (2023) places Belgium among the education systems that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities, the indicator behind Figure B9, which covers national curricula, assessment documents and rules obliging schools to provide tuition in a named language. No regional or minority language subject provision is recorded for it there.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.CA|Newfoundland and Labrador: Not established from the sources consulted. No provincial Indigenous language course appears in the cited curriculum pages.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.CU|Cuba: Not established from the sources consulted. The 2019 Constitution names no language but Spanish and no language subject, and PEER publishes no Inclusion chapter for Cuba against which that could be checked.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.DM|Dominica: Not established from the sources consulted. No Kwéyòl or Kalinago subject appears in the sources cited on this entry.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.GD|Grenada: Not established from the sources consulted. The sources on this entry are Caribbean Examinations Council, CSEC Modern Languages syllabus, CXC 27/0/SYLL 05 and SUMMA (Laboratory for Research and Innovation in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean), Grenada country review. No vernacular language subject appears in the sources cited on this entry.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.IS|Iceland: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key data on teaching languages at school in Europe (2023) places Iceland among the education systems that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities, the indicator behind Figure B9, which covers national curricula, assessment documents and rules obliging schools to provide tuition in a named language. No regional or minority language subject provision is recorded for it there.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.KG|Kyrgyzstan: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER Kyrgyzstan inclusion profile and Ferrando (2020) were read in full and neither records a minority language as a timetabled subject; the Education Development Strategy 2012-20 action plan names only Kyrgyz, Russian and English as subject curricula to be developed. The consolidated Law on Education on cbd.minjust.gov.kg could not be retrieved (the page returns a JavaScript shell with no legal text).
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.LI|Liechtenstein: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key Data on Teaching Languages at School in Europe (2023 edition, policy position 2021/22) lists Liechtenstein among the countries that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities. Its Figure B9 records no reference for Liechtenstein, and German is its sole state language on Figure A1.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.LS|Lesotho: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Lesotho describes Sesotho only as the initial medium of instruction before an unspecified switch to English in upper primary; it says nothing about Sesotho as a timetabled subject, which years it runs, or whether it is compulsory. Searched: PEER Lesotho inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.LU|Luxembourg: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key data on teaching languages at school in Europe (2023) places Luxembourg among the education systems that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities, the indicator behind Figure B9, which covers national curricula, assessment documents and rules obliging schools to provide tuition in a named language. No regional or minority language subject provision is recorded for it there.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.MG|Madagascar: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Madagascar describes the Education Sector Plan 2018-2022 only in terms of mother-tongue reading before a second language and of managing dialect-French bilingualism; it names no timetabled Malagasy or dialect subject, no years and no optionality, and records that the language policy itself is still to be defined. Searched: PEER Madagascar inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.MN|Mongolia: Not established from the sources consulted. The 2019 CERD session records the government supporting bilingual education of the Kazakh and Tuva minorities and treating ethnic minority languages as intangible heritage to be preserved, and PEER records a right of free access to pre-primary and primary education in the mother tongue and an ADB project improving Kazakh-language textbooks; neither names the language as a timetabled subject.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.MR|Mauritania: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Mauritania mentions Fula, Soninke and Wolof only as constitutionally named national languages whose 'promotion' higher-education law allows alongside Arabic-medium teaching; it does not say whether any of them is a timetabled school subject, in which years, or on what terms. Searched: PEER Mauritania inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.MT|Malta: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key Data on Teaching Languages at School in Europe (2023 edition, policy position 2021/22) lists Malta among the countries that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities. Maltese and English are both state languages on the same source's Figure A1, so neither is carried on this map as a regional or minority subject.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.MW|Malawi: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Malawi covers Chichewa only as a permitted medium under the 2013 Education Act, and notes nationwide Chichewa textbook distribution plus piloted mother-tongue projects awaiting scale-up; it describes no timetabled Malawian-language subject, no year range and no optionality. Searched: PEER Malawi inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.QA|Qatar: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER inclusion profile for Qatar records that there is no explicit mention of any linguistic or ethnic minorities, and the only curriculum content it names in that connection is the 2017-22 ministry strategy's aim of fostering respect for other cultures.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.SC|Seychelles: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Seychelles gives the Creole medium-of-instruction rule and the 2013-17 education strategic plan's aim of increasing cultural diversity, but does not say whether Kreol Seselwa is separately timetabled as a subject after P3, for which years, or whether it is compulsory. Searched: PEER Seychelles inclusion profile.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.TM|Turkmenistan: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Law's article on languages of training and education makes foreign languages obligatory subjects in general and professional programmes, but provides for the native language only as state assistance to citizens studying it under other legislation, and names no such language as a school subject.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.VC|Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act 2006 names no Garifuna, Creole or vernacular subject at any level, and the Garifuna Heritage Foundation's 2024 programme describes training workshops for teachers and cultural exchanges rather than language classes.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.YE|Yemen: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER Yemen inclusion profile was read in full; it lists Sokotri, Mehri and Hobyot among languages spoken by small linguistic communities but records no language subject other than English as a second language from primary school onwards. No Yemeni education law or curriculum document naming these languages was retrieved.
indigenous.taughtAsSubject.ZM|Zambia: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Zambia sets out the 2013 Curriculum Framework only as a medium-of-instruction rule for Grades 1-4, and records the 2011-15 sector plan's proposal to review the policy 'to promote the teaching of local languages at primary level'; neither passage describes a timetabled Zambian-language subject, its years, or whether it is optional. Searched: PEER Zambia inclusion profile.

indigenous.revitalisation.AF|Afghanistan: Not established from the sources consulted. Art. 16 of the 2004 Constitution obliges the state to design and apply effective programs to foster and develop all languages of Afghanistan, but names no programme, body, start date or funding; the UNESCO GEM Report PEER inclusion profile for Afghanistan records only that school books are produced in two national languages and in several minority languages, and it describes the framework as it stood before August 2021.
indigenous.revitalisation.AG|Antigua and Barbuda: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act 2008 mentions language only in the goal of promoting understanding of the history, language, culture, rights and values of Antigua and Barbuda, and carries no maintenance, documentation or promotion programme for any language; UNESCO PEER’s ethnic and linguistic groups section for the country is about care in assessing the special educational needs of children whose first language is not English.
indigenous.revitalisation.BB|Barbados: Not established from the sources consulted. The Ministry of Education's own Reimagining Education in Barbados reform paper proposes only functional foreign languages as a curricular addition and names no promotion, academy or programme for the local vernacular. The Education Act, Cap. 41 (L.R.O. 1997, as amended) uses the word language only three times, each of them in an offence provision about insulting, abusive or indecent language to a teacher or school attendance officer, and carries no language-of-education or language-promotion clause at all.
indigenous.revitalisation.BH|Bahrain: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER inclusion profile for Bahrain gives, under 'Ethnic and linguistic groups', only Constitution Art. 7 on pride in Arabism and Bahrain's adoption of the 2007 UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and the TIMSS 2023 Encyclopedia chapter for Bahrain records Arabic as the official language and the language of instruction in all public schools; neither names any language-promotion or revitalisation activity, actor, start date or funding.
indigenous.revitalisation.DO|Dominican Republic: Not established from the sources consulted. Ley 66-97, Ley General de Educación, names lengua only in generic curricular aims - expression in the lengua materna, the basics of at least one lengua extranjera, the value of a command of lenguas - and establishes no body, programme or funding to promote any named language. Ley 139-01 on higher education, science and technology contains no occurrence of lengua or idioma at all. The UNESCO PEER profile cited on this entry can no longer be read: education-profiles.org now serves only an archive notice pointing to the new PEER site, which has no Dominican Republic page at the paths tried.
indigenous.revitalisation.GD|Grenada: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Act, Cap. 86, was read end to end: it names language only in its statement of goals, at goal (g) on knowledge and understanding of the history, language, culture, rights and values of Grenadians, and in its offence and teacher-qualification sections, and it sets up no body, programme or funding for any language. SUMMA's Grenada country review records one language activity, a local programme called Spice Signs teaching sign language on the Government Information Station daily since the onset of COVID-19, which it frames as support for children with special needs rather than as reversing language shift; it records nothing on a Grenadian vernacular.
indigenous.revitalisation.GW|Guinea-Bissau: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER Guinea-Bissau inclusion profile names only the National Literacy and Non-Formal Education Policy's aim to develop a language policy document and to promote Portuguese, Creole and national languages as languages of education, learning and professional qualification, with no implementing body, no start date and no funding attached. Lopes, drawing on four exploratory interviews with Guinean students, treats the non-officialisation of Creole as an open question and argues the State should consider valorising it; he names no current programme. Searched: PEER Guinea-Bissau inclusion profile; Lopes, UNILAB repository.
indigenous.revitalisation.KN|Saint Kitts and Nevis: Not established from the sources consulted. The Ministry of Education Language Policy of 3 June 2018 sets a language awareness approach inside the classroom and names no documentation, maintenance or promotion activity for the dialect beyond schooling; UNESCO PEER’s ethnic and linguistic groups section for Saint Kitts and Nevis is about learners emigrating from the Dominican Republic for whom English is not a first language.
indigenous.revitalisation.KW|Kuwait: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER inclusion profile for Kuwait says, under 'Ethnic and linguistic groups', only that Arabic is the only language of instruction at all levels and that English is taught to all children as a second language, and the TIMSS 2023 Encyclopedia chapter for Kuwait records Arabic as the official language of instruction throughout all stages of education; neither names any activity, body, start date or funding for reversing language shift.
indigenous.revitalisation.LA|Laos: Not established from the sources consulted. The Education Law (Art. 44) makes Lao language and Lao script the official languages for teaching and learning, and Art. 45 covers only foreign languages, naming no ethnic-group language and no measure to maintain one; the UNESCO GEM Report PEER inclusion profile's section on ethnic and language groups records only extending distance learning for minority groups and teaching Lao as a second language to ethnic minority children, with the official national language remaining the medium of instruction. Neither document names a body, a date or any funding for reversing language shift.
indigenous.revitalisation.LI|Liechtenstein: Not established from the sources consulted. The Advisory Committee's Fifth Opinion on Liechtenstein (ACFC, adopted 1 February 2021) records that on depositing its instrument of ratification Liechtenstein declared that no national minorities in the sense of the Framework Convention exist in its territory, and that it made a similar declaration on ratifying the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages; the Opinion describes anti-discrimination, hate-speech and integration measures but no language revitalisation or language-promotion measure, no body running one, no start date and no funding. Eurydice's Key data on teaching languages at school in Europe (2023 edition, policy position 2021/22) lists German as Liechtenstein's only state language on Figure A1 with no regional or minority language of official status, and the report describes no promotion measure for Liechtenstein anywhere in its text. Neither document addresses any measure for German itself.
indigenous.revitalisation.MG|Madagascar: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNICEF/Trudell 2017 country review for Madagascar sets out the language policy, the education policy and the studies feeding the Education Sector Plan 2018-2022, and the only language-policy activity it names is a national seminar on language policy in education organised by the French embassy; it names no programme, body, start date or funding for reversing shift in Malagasy or its varieties. The UNESCO PEER Madagascar inclusion profile describes only the sector plan's reading, mother-tongue transition and plurilingual aims, and records that provision is made for adopting a new language policy. Searched: Trudell 2017 Madagascar country review; PEER Madagascar inclusion profile.
indigenous.revitalisation.OM|Oman: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER inclusion profile for Oman covers, under 'Ethnic minorities and indigenous students', only free education for residents and the right of foreign communities to establish their own schools, and the PIRLS 2021 Encyclopedia chapter for Oman names Swahili, Baluchi, Lawati and Jabali as other spoken languages without recording any provision for them; neither names any activity, body, start date or funding for reversing language shift.
indigenous.revitalisation.SX|Sint Maarten: Not established from the sources consulted. The Landsverordening officiële talen was read in full, all eight articles: it fixes English and Dutch as the official languages, governs which of them the government uses with residents, and empowers rules on their spelling, but sets out no promotion, revival or maintenance measure and names no other language. The Ministry's 2022 Sint Maarten Education Review discusses language only as a medium-of-instruction and pupil-proficiency problem, recommending that schools develop language policies that take account of pupils' varying native languages; it names no revitalisation activity, actor or funding.
